issues.legal_issue: A government registration-fee schedule is not invalid merely because the proceeds enter the consolidated fund or the fee charged to an individual is not proportionate to the services received by that individual, where the challenge does not establish a lack of reasonable aggregate correlation between total receipts and the cost of registration services.
material_facts: The government prescribed registration fees on a graduated scale based on the value of the subject matter of the instrument.

The claimants challenged the schedule after paying a registration fee to register a mortgage deed, arguing that the fee was a tax because the government had not shown that the proceeds were separately appropriated for registration services.
The lower courts considered the fee paid by the claimants but did not examine total registration-fee receipts against the overall cost of maintaining and operating the registration department.
There was no material showing that the department’s total fee receipts substantially exceeded its overall expenditure.
issues.conclusion: The fee schedule could not be invalidated on the grounds that the proceeds were not kept in a separate fund or that the fee paid by the claimants was not individually matched to services rendered to them. The appeal was allowed, the judgments below were set aside, and the suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 78 of the Registration Act, the State Government may prescribe registration fees. Applying Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Mohd. Yasin, Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti v. Orient Paper & Industries Ltd., Secretary to Government of Madras v. P.R. Sriramulu, and Bombay Stock Exchange Brokers’ Forum v. Securities and Exchange Board of India, the court held that a fee requires a reasonable, broadly assessed correlation between the levy and the services, not mathematical exactitude or a direct individual quid pro quo. Article 266 of the Constitution requires government revenues, including fees, to be credited to the relevant Consolidated Fund, so separate appropriation is not essential to a fee. The stricter approach in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt had been modified by later decisions; decisions relying on that approach to require strict correlation or separate appropriation were overruled.

predicates.registration_fee_schedule_challenged: A party brought a proceeding challenging the validity of a government schedule prescribing registration fees.
predicates.government_registration_services_provide: The government maintained registration services and incurred costs in providing them.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_individual_service_m: The challenge relied on the fee paid by an individual not matching the services received by that individual, or on the proceeds not being kept in a separate fund for those services.
predicates.aggregate_receipts_not_shown_to_substant: The record did not show that total fee receipts substantially exceeded the overall cost of providing the relevant services.

issues.definition: When a registration-fee schedule is challenged, and the challenge rests on individual service mismatch or the absence of a separate fund without showing that aggregate receipts substantially exceed service costs, the schedule is not invalidated on those grounds.
